passage: Salma Apa, you know your Asif. Put me in a crowded room and I light up. Cricket after school, chai at the corner, the group call till midnight, I say yes to all of it. When everyone goes home and the house goes quiet, I feel flat, like a phone at two percent. Last Saturday some older boys from tuition said they were riding to the highway dhaba at night, three to a bike, no helmets. Everyone said yes, so I said yes too, before I'd even thought. Halfway there I felt sick about it and made them drop me at the petrol pump. I called Abbu to fetch me. He didn't shout; he just said, "Next time, call before." I think I say yes because I'm scared of the quiet, not because I want to go.

qa.q: Where did the older boys say they were riding at night?
qa.a: To the highway dhaba, three to a bike, no helmets.

qa.q: What does Asif think lies behind saying yes to every plan?
qa.a: Asif thinks the yeses come from being scared of the quiet, not from really wanting to go.

qa.q: What choice did Asif make halfway to the dhaba?
qa.a: Asif asked to be dropped at the petrol pump and called Abbu, stepping out of a risky plan.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when that call came?
qa.a: He was probably worried but relieved; he stayed calm and only asked to be called earlier next time.

grounding: A teenager who feels alive in company and flat alone notices that saying yes to everything led toward a risky ride.

passage:
Swati is the first to reply in our class group, every time. Movie on Friday? Yes. Garba practice? Yes. Helping the seniors with their fest stall till nine? Yes. She seems to glow in a crowd; I've seen her get a whole bus singing. But when her friends were all away at weddings in the holidays, she posted a photo of an empty room captioned "so bored" and messaged me eleven times in an hour. Last week the fest seniors asked her to copy their attendance sheet for them, and she did, though I saw her hesitate first. I don't know what she was feeling. Maybe she just didn't want them to stop inviting her. I told her she could say no to me anytime and I'd still save her a seat.
Maria

qa.q: How many times did Swati message Maria in an hour?
qa.a: She messaged Maria eleven times in an hour.

qa.q: Why might Swati have agreed to copy the seniors' attendance sheet even though she hesitated?
qa.a: Maria guesses she didn't want them to stop inviting her; the wish to stay included may have outweighed her doubt.

qa.q: What choice did Maria make after seeing Swati hesitate?
qa.a: Maria told Swati she could say no anytime and still have a saved seat, making refusing feel safer.

qa.q: How might Maria feel watching Swati say yes to everything?
qa.a: Maria seems concerned and unsure, having noticed Swati's hesitation and the eleven messages, which is why Maria offers a seat with no conditions.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl who glows in company and feels flat alone, and sees her need for company slide into pleasing older students.

passage: Arnab, you think I don't understand why you can't stay home one Saturday? At sixteen your Hafsa Khala was a girl just like you. In Kolkata I said yes to every plan: cricket on the maidan, every wedding, every adda at the tea stall. An empty Sunday made me feel like a switched-off fan. One Puja night my crowd went up to a friend's terrace. Music, laughter, everyone daring each other to sit on the parapet for a photo, four floors up. I was next. They were chanting my name, and I wanted them to keep liking me more than I wanted anything. Then I looked down. I said, 'No. I'm going home.' They booed. Two of them walked me down anyway, and I told my father that night; by morning the terrace door had a lock. I still loved crowds, Arnab. I just stopped letting them choose for me.

qa.q: What were Hafsa's friends daring each other to do?
qa.a: To sit on the parapet of a terrace four floors up for a photo.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as everyone chanted her name?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a strong pull to please them, wanting to be liked more than anything, with fear rising as she looked down.

qa.q: What turning point in Hafsa's story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Looking down and saying 'No, I'm going home'; Hafsa chose safety over the crowd's approval, and then told her father so the terrace was locked.

qa.q: How might the two friends who walked Hafsa down have seen her choice?
qa.a: They may have respected it, or felt relieved themselves, since they chose to leave the chanting and go with Hafsa.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager who feels most alive in a crowd and says yes to everything, until the pull to please nearly leads into danger.

passage: By Saturday afternoon Yusuf had said yes to three things: cricket at four, Sachin's science model at five, Farah's birthday at six. He had never been good at no. At the ground, some older boys were heading to the lake on their bikes. 'Come, Yusuf, you're fun.' He felt the warm rush of being wanted, and went, his phone buzzing in his pocket. At the lake they dared each other to jump off the old jetty; Yusuf laughed along but stayed on the planks, suddenly unsure. When he checked his phone it was seven: four missed calls from Sachin and a photo of a half-built model. He had missed the birthday too. At home that night, alone, the house felt flat and grey. He typed 'sorry' to Sachin, deleted it, and typed it again.

qa.q: What had Yusuf said yes to for Saturday?
qa.a: Cricket at four, Sachin's science model at five and Farah's birthday at six.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel when the older boys said 'you're fun'?
qa.a: He felt a warm rush of being wanted, which pulled him along even though he had promised Sachin.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try before saying yes next time?
qa.a: Check what he has already promised and say 'not today' to new plans, keeping his word to friends like Sachin.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for Sachin?
qa.a: Sachin was left building the model alone, calling four times, probably hurt and let down.

grounding: Shows a teenager who says yes to every plan and feels flat alone, whose need for company slides into letting a friend down and drifting toward risk.

passage: The flat in Madhapur went silent after his parents left for a wedding in Vizag, and within an hour Naveen felt like a phone on two percent. He messaged six people. Zainab replied first: 'Studying, sorry! Tomorrow?' The only yes came from the seniors' group: 'Come over. Bring your laptop.' He went, and it was loud and bright, and he felt alive again. Around ten one of them said, 'Naveen, you're good at essays, na? Do ours for Monday? You're one of us now.' Everyone looked at him. He heard himself say, 'Sure, no problem.' Walking home, the glow faded. Three essays, and his own not started. Zainab called. 'Why do you sound weird?' He told her. 'Would they still invite you if you said no?' she asked. He didn't know. That was the worst part.

qa.q: What did the seniors ask Naveen to do?
qa.a: Write their essays for Monday.

qa.q: Why did Naveen say 'Sure, no problem'?
qa.a: He felt alive and wanted in the group, and was afraid that saying no would cost him that belonging.

qa.q: What could Naveen say to the seniors now?
qa.a: He could tell them honestly that he won't write their essays, and find out whether they still invite him, as Zainab's question suggests.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel hearing Naveen's story?
qa.a: Zainab seems concerned for him, asking a gentle question so he sees the cost of saying yes to everything.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels flat alone and alive in a crowd, and whose need for company slides into peer-pleasing.

passage:
"Nazia, you're going to Kabir's farmhouse party tonight? After the fair and the movie?"
"Obviously, Reena. Everyone's going."
"You've said yes to every plan this month. Are you even tired?"
"Tired is better than sitting at home. When I'm alone I feel flat, like switched off."
"Okay. But how are you getting there?"
"Arjun's driving. He just got his licence."
"The one who raced his bike at the flyover?"
Nazia paused. "Everyone's going with him."
"So would you go if nobody asked you?"
A long silence. "Maybe not with Arjun."
"Come to mine instead. Movie night. My cousins are coming, it'll be loud."
Nazia laughed. "Loud is good. Okay. I'll text them I'm not coming."

qa.q: Who was going to drive to the farmhouse party?
qa.a: Arjun, who just got his licence.

qa.q: How does Nazia feel when she is alone?
qa.a: Nazia feels flat, as if switched off.

qa.q: How did Reena help Nazia avoid a risky choice?
qa.a: She asked whether Nazia really wanted to go, pointed out the risky driver and offered a loud gathering at home instead.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Nazia agrees to come over?
qa.a: Reena may feel relieved and glad, knowing Nazia chose company without the risk.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels most alive in company and says yes to every plan, with a friend showing where peer-pleasing could slide into risk.
